🌍 US attacks caused severe environmental pollution in southern Iran: Official

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Head of Iran’s Department of Environment Shina Ansari says attacks on fuel storage tanks and facilities in Assaluyeh, a Persian Gulf port city in southern Iran, caused massive air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Ansari made the remarks at a conference on ecocide and silent war crimes in Tehran on Sunday, stressing that the environmental consequences of military attacks extend far beyond the battlefield and can affect human health and ecosystems for decades.
​
The official said attacks on fuel storage tanks and facilities in Assaluyeh released around 904 metric tons of particulate matter, 4,700 metric tons of volatile compounds and more than 13,000 metric tons of sulfur oxides, while 1.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide entered the atmosphere.
​
The destruction of energy infrastructure not only threatens public health but also undermines national efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and protect the environment, she noted.
​
Ansari called for climate justice and international accountability for environmental damage caused by military conflicts, stressing the need to document the damage and assess its short- and long-term consequences.
​
The conference also unveiled the first collection of legal and environmental reports, comprising 133 items, for submission to international forums.

⚡️ Iran’s foreign minister: Environment must not be used as tool of political pressure

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the environment is a shared heritage of humanity and must not be used as a tool of political pressure or sacrificed to short-term economic and military interests, stressing the importance of international law in protecting the environment during armed conflicts.

“The environment is the common heritage of humanity. It must not become an arena for rivalries, a tool of political pressure, or a casualty of short-term economic and military interests,” Araghchi said while addressing the International Conference on “Ecocide, A Silent War Crime” in Tehran on Sunday.
​
He described ecocide, or the large-scale destruction of the environment during armed conflicts, as one of the most serious challenges facing humanity, saying it is inextricably linked to the right to life, human health, food security, international peace and security, and the rights of future generations.
​
“Today, the environment can no longer be regarded as the silent victim of war. Wars and armed conflicts do not merely claim human lives and destroy cities and economic and social infrastructure; they also expose water, soil, air, forests, agricultural land, energy resources, natural habitats, and biodiversity to devastating impacts,” the foreign minister said.
​
He added that the destruction of water and soil resources, air pollution, the loss of vegetation and ecosystems, and the release of pollutants, waste, and hazardous materials could persist for years or even decades after conflicts end.
​
Araghchi cited the wars in Iran, Lebanon, and Gaza as recent examples of conflicts that have inflicted devastating environmental damage through attacks on energy facilities, sewage and water treatment plants, farmland, gardens, and coastlines.
​
“These are not merely economic losses. When a military attack causes lasting soil contamination, damages water resources, destroys forests, pollutes the air and sea, and generates hazardous materials and remnants of war, its consequences can extend far beyond the time and place of the attack,” he said, adding, “From this perspective, peace, security, the environment, public health, and climate change are not separate issues. The links between them must receive greater attention than ever before.”
​
The foreign minister also outlined Iran’s position, saying that, from the perspective of the Islamic Republic, “international law must not remain indifferent to environmental destruction and violations of fundamental human rights during wartime.”
​
He stressed that, alongside the effective implementation of international humanitarian law, the direct and indirect environmental consequences of military actions must also be taken into account.
​
Araghchi said all countries must fulfill their international obligations regarding environmental destruction. He also emphasized that the environment must be protected during armed conflicts without allowing such protection to become a pretext for double standards or for granting concessions to some countries while imposing obligations on others.
​
Furthermore, he said, unilateral coercive measures and restrictions that hinder countries’ access to financial resources, technologies, and essential equipment needed to protect the environment must be seriously examined in light of international law and their human and environmental consequences.
​
Araghchi said Iran was ready to contribute to collective efforts to prevent large-scale environmental destruction, strengthen regional cooperation, and promote the fulfillment of international responsibilities.
